title: Prompt Engineering for Content & Sales
subtitle: Structured prompts, context packs, templates and guardrails for on-brand content, outreach, call prep, follow-ups and proposals
description:
Most AI output is generic because most prompts are vague and most assistants are missing context. This intermediate course teaches creators, marketers and sales professionals to write prompts that work like professional briefs, and to turn the best into a reusable team system.

You'll master a six-part prompt structure, examples and output formats, targeted refinement and techniques for sharper thinking, then build a context pack (voice guide, offer sheet, approved claims, customer language) in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft 365 Copilot or Notion AI. You'll use templates for hooks, captions, scripts and long-form chains, and sales prompts for prospect research, outreach, call prep, follow-ups, proposals and objection handling, all with guardrails against invented claims and fake urgency. Finally, you'll evaluate with the CLEAR rubric, escape generic AI style, and build a shared prompt library with saved assistants and safe automations. Every lesson includes copy-paste prompts with before-and-after results and a detailed video lecture.
outcomes: Write structured prompts using role, context, task, constraints, examples and output format
Refine drafts with targeted feedback and use reasoning, perspectives and chains for better thinking
Build a context pack in a project, GPT, Gem or notebook so outputs use approved facts and voice
Use content templates and long-form prompt chains for posts, newsletters, case studies and landing pages
Research prospects and write relevant outreach, call prep, follow-ups, proposals and objection responses
Evaluate and fact-check outputs with the CLEAR rubric and a reviewer setup before publishing or sending
Build a versioned team prompt library with saved assistants and draft-only automations

lessons.title: The six-part prompt: role, context, task, constraints, examples, format
lessons.body:
### Prompts are briefs

The biggest shift in prompting is to stop thinking of a prompt as a question and start thinking of it as a **creative brief**. If you handed a freelancer the sentence "write a caption for my bakery", you would get something generic. If you gave them your audience, your offer, your tone and the platform, you would get something usable. AI works the same way.

A reliable structure has six parts. You will not always need all six, but checking against them fixes most weak prompts.

### 1. Role

Tell the model what expertise to bring. "You are a senior direct-response copywriter who specializes in Instagram ads for food brands in the Gulf." A role nudges vocabulary, priorities and standards. Keep it relevant; "world's greatest genius" adds nothing.

### 2. Context

This is where most prompts fail. Include:

- **Who you are:** brand, product, price point, positioning.
- **Audience:** who they are, what they want, what they worry about, what language they use.
- **Situation:** campaign goal, platform, season, what has worked before.
- **Facts the model must use:** approved claims, prices, dates.

### 3. Task

One clear verb and deliverable: "Write five caption options", "Rewrite this email", "Summarize these reviews into three themes". If you have several tasks, number them or split them into separate prompts.

### 4. Constraints

The rules: length, tone, words to avoid, compliance requirements, reading level, language variety (British or American English, Gulf or Levantine Arabic, Urdu or Roman Urdu).

Examples: "Under 150 characters before the 'more' cut-off." "No health claims." "Do not use the words 'elevate', 'unlock' or 'game-changer'." "Include #ad at the start because this is a paid partnership."

### 5. Examples

Show, don't just tell. One or two examples of captions you love, or past posts that performed well, teach tone faster than any adjective. (More on this in the next lesson.)

### 6. Output format

Say exactly how you want the answer: a numbered list, a table with columns, a script with timestamps, JSON for a spreadsheet, or "hook on line one, body, then CTA".

### Before and after

**Weak:** "Write a caption for my bakery's new cake."

**Strong:**

> **Role:** You are a social media copywriter for independent food brands in Pakistan.
> **Context:** We are Crumb & Co, a home bakery in Lahore selling custom cakes (from PKR 4,500). Audience: women aged 25–40 planning birthdays, who order via WhatsApp. Our tone is warm, playful and slightly cheeky. We are launching a pistachio-rose cake for Eid.
> **Task:** Write five Instagram caption options for the launch Reel.
> **Constraints:** Each under 60 words. First line must work as a hook on its own. Mix English with light Roman Urdu. No claims about being "the best in Lahore". End with a CTA to WhatsApp.
> **Example of our voice:** "Birthday on Saturday and zero plan? Relax, jaan. We've got the cake. You bring the candles."
> **Format:** Numbered list, each option followed by a one-line note on the angle used.

The second prompt takes two extra minutes to write and saves twenty minutes of editing.

### Where the six parts live in 2026 assistants

You don't have to type all six parts every time. Modern assistants let you store the stable parts once:

| Part | Stable or per-task? | Where to store it |
|---|---|---|
| Role | Mostly stable | Project instructions, a custom GPT, a Gemini Gem, Claude project instructions |
| Context | Brand context stable; campaign context per task | Project files (voice guide, product sheet) + a few lines per task |
| Task | Per task | The prompt |
| Constraints | Brand rules stable; task limits per task | Project instructions + the prompt |
| Examples | Mostly stable | Project files ("best posts", "best emails") |
| Format | Per task, or saved defaults | The prompt, or project instructions for defaults |

With a well-built project, your everyday prompt shrinks to task, task-specific context and format, and the output still reflects all six parts.

### Hands-on: rebuild one of your own prompts

Take the last prompt you used for content or sales. Paste it into this checker:

```text
Here is a prompt I used: [paste].
Check it against six parts: role, context, task, constraints, examples, output format.
For each part: present / missing / weak, and one specific improvement.
Then rewrite the prompt with the improvements, using [PLACEHOLDERS] for facts only I can supply.
Do not invent facts about my business.
```

**Before:** "Write a LinkedIn post about our new HR software feature."

**After:** a structured prompt with a role (B2B SaaS content writer for HR leaders), context (the feature, the audience's pain in their words, one approved customer result as [PROOF]), a single task, constraints (under 180 words, first line under 12 words, no "revolutionary"), one example post, and a format (hook, 3 short paragraphs, question to prompt comments). Fill the placeholders and you'll typically go from four rounds of editing to one.

### Quick checklist

Before you hit enter, ask:

- Would a human freelancer understand exactly what I want?
- Did I give facts the model cannot guess?
- Did I say what to avoid?
- Did I specify the format I need?

### Pitfalls

- **Over-stuffing:** a two-page prompt full of irrelevant history can dilute the key instructions. Put the most important rules near the task, and keep context relevant.
- **Conflicting instructions:** "Be concise" and "include every detail" pull in opposite directions. Decide which wins.
- **Relying on role alone:** "You are an expert marketer" without context still produces generic work.

video.script:
Here's the single biggest upgrade you can make to your AI results. Stop writing questions. Start writing briefs.

Think about it. If you told a freelance copywriter, write a caption for my bakery, you'd get something bland. But if you told them who your customers are, what you're launching, how your brand sounds, and what to avoid, you'd get something you could actually post. AI works exactly the same way.

A great prompt has six parts.

One. Role. Tell the model what expertise to bring, like a social media copywriter for food brands in Pakistan.

Two. Context. Who you are, who your audience is, what the campaign is for, and the facts it must use. This is where most prompts fall short.

Three. Task. One clear deliverable. Write five caption options.

Four. Constraints. Length, tone, banned words, and compliance rules, like including hashtag ad on paid partnerships.

Five. Examples. Paste a caption you love. One real example teaches tone faster than a list of adjectives.

Six. Output format. A numbered list, a table, a script with timestamps. Say exactly what you need.

You won't need all six every time. But when an output disappoints, run through this list, and you'll usually find the missing piece.

A strong prompt might take two extra minutes to write. It routinely saves twenty minutes of editing. That's the trade we're going to practice throughout this course.

lessons.title: Using examples and output formats to control results
lessons.body:
### Why examples are so powerful

Language models are exceptional pattern-followers. When you include examples in your prompt, a technique often called **few-shot prompting**, you give the model a concrete pattern to match. It is the fastest way to transfer tone, structure and quality standards.

Compare these two instructions:

- "Write in a friendly, confident, slightly witty tone."
- "Here are two captions in our voice: [example 1] [example 2]. Write three more in the same voice."

The second almost always wins, because "friendly, confident, witty" means different things to different people, while the examples show exactly what you mean.

### How to use examples well

1. **Use your best real work.** Past posts that performed well, emails that got replies, scripts your audience loved.
2. **Show variety within the pattern.** Two or three examples that differ in topic but share voice teach the model what to keep constant.
3. **Label them clearly.** "Example 1 (Reel caption, product launch):" helps the model understand what each is.
4. **Say what to copy and what not to.** "Match the tone and structure, not the topic or specific phrases." Otherwise the model may reuse your exact lines.
5. **Use counter-examples sparingly.** "Here is a caption we dislike because it sounds salesy: [...]. Avoid this style." This can sharpen boundaries.

### Output formats that save editing time

Asking for a specific structure makes the output easier to review, compare and paste into other tools.

**Numbered options with rationale**
"Give 10 hooks as a numbered list. After each, add in brackets the psychological angle (curiosity, fear of missing out, social proof, contrarian)."

**Tables**
"Create a 2-week content calendar as a table with columns: Date, Platform, Format, Hook, Key message, CTA."

**Scripts with timing**
"Write a 40-second Reel script in three columns: Time, Visual, Voiceover. Keep the voiceover under 100 words."

**Structured for other tools**
"Return the result as CSV with headers: subject_line, preview_text, angle", for pasting into a spreadsheet or email platform.

**Fixed templates**
"Use exactly this structure: HOOK (1 line) / PROBLEM (2 lines) / SOLUTION (2 lines) / PROOF (1 line) / CTA (1 line)."

### Worked example: email subject lines

A UK online fashion boutique wants subject lines for a summer sale.

> Here are three past subject lines with high open rates for our audience (women 25–45, UK, value-conscious but style-led):
> 1. "The linen edit you asked for (finally)"
> 2. "Your Saturday outfit, sorted"
> 3. "We restocked the dress. Yes, that one."
> Match their voice: conversational, specific, a little knowing, no shouting. Avoid ALL CAPS, excessive emojis and the word "SALE" in the first three words.
> Task: write 12 subject lines for our summer sale (up to 40% off selected lines, ends Sunday).
> Format: table with columns Subject line, Preview text (under 90 characters), Angle.

The result is consistent, on-brand and easy to shortlist. The team then tests the top options with their email platform's A/B feature.

### Hands-on: build an example bank in 20 minutes

Examples are your strongest lever, so keep them organized. Create a document (or project file) called **Example bank** with labeled sections:

```text
EXAMPLE BANK - [Brand]
## Reel captions (top performers)
Example 1 (product launch, [date], [result e.g. 3x usual saves]): ...
Example 2 (behind the scenes): ...
## Email subject lines (highest open rates)
...
## Sales emails that got replies
...
## Counter-examples (don't sound like this)
...
```

Then reference it in prompts:

```text
Using the "Reel captions" examples in the attached Example bank, write 5 captions for [topic].
Match tone, sentence length and structure, not topics or phrases. Do not reuse any phrase of 4+ words from the examples.
Format: table - Caption | Angle | Why it fits the examples.
```

**Before:** "Write captions in a friendly, witty tone" returns the model's idea of "witty" (puns, exclamation marks).

**After:** captions with your real rhythm (short, dry, specific), because the model matched your top performers instead of an adjective.

### Structured outputs for your tools

When output goes into a spreadsheet, scheduler or CRM, ask for a machine-friendly format and test it once:

```text
Return only CSV with headers: date,platform,hook,caption,cta,hashtags. Quote any field containing commas.
```

If your assistant supports it, ask for a table you can export, or paste the CSV into a sheet and check that every column landed correctly before scaling up.

### Pitfalls

- **Copying examples too closely.** If outputs repeat your example phrases, add "Do not reuse phrases from the examples."
- **Examples that break your own rules.** If your example includes a claim you no longer make, the model will copy it.
- **Too many examples.** Beyond a handful, returns diminish and prompts get long. Choose your best.
- **Format without substance.** A beautiful table of weak ideas is still weak. Format supports thinking; it does not replace context.

### Mini-template

> Here are [2–3] examples of [content type] in our voice:
> [examples, labeled]
> Match their [tone/structure/length], but not their topics or exact phrases.
> Now write [number] [content type] about [topic] for [audience].
> Format: [list/table/script columns].

scenes.narration: What does witty mean? To you, it might mean dry, understated and specific. To the AI, it might mean puns and three exclamation marks. That gap is why so many people describe their brand voice perfectly and still get output that sounds nothing like them. In this lecture you'll learn the fastest fix in all of prompt engineering: examples. And its partner: output formats, which make results easier to review and paste into your tools. You'll see a UK boutique's subject lines, an example bank for a skincare brand, and watch me turn adjectives into examples live.

scenes.narration: Think of it like asking a band to play something in the style of your favorite artist. You could describe it: upbeat but a bit moody, with a strong chorus. Or you could just play them two tracks. Two tracks work better than one, because the band can hear what's consistent across both, the style, and what's specific to each, the song. That's why two or three varied examples beat a single example. And you'd add: same style, new song. Don't copy the melody. In prompts, that's: match the tone and structure, not the topic or specific phrases.

lessons.title: Refine, don't restart: the feedback loop
lessons.body:
### The first answer is a starting point

Professionals rarely accept a first draft from a human writer, and they should not from AI either. The real skill is **iterative refinement**: giving specific, targeted feedback that moves the output closer to what you need.

### Vague vs specific feedback

| Vague (weak) | Specific (strong) |
|---|---|
| "Make it better." | "The hook is too slow. Start with the customer's problem in under 8 words." |
| "More engaging." | "Add one concrete detail from a customer's life, such as the school run or a late-night craving." |
| "Too long." | "Cut to 80 words. Keep the second and fourth sentences." |
| "Not our tone." | "Less formal. Use contractions, short sentences and one light joke. Remove 'we are delighted'." |

Specific feedback tells the model what to change, how and what to keep.

### A five-move refinement toolkit

1. **Select and build:** "Option 3 is closest. Write five variations of option 3 with different opening lines."
2. **Surgical edit:** "Keep everything except the CTA. Rewrite the CTA to push WhatsApp orders, not website visits."
3. **Dial a quality:** "Make it 30% more playful" or "Make it more premium: fewer exclamation marks, more sensory detail."
4. **Change the angle:** "Rewrite from the perspective of a customer who was skeptical at first."
5. **Critique then revise:** "Before rewriting, list three weaknesses of this draft from the perspective of a busy mum scrolling Instagram. Then fix them."

### Ask the model to critique itself

Models are often better at spotting problems when explicitly asked to evaluate. Useful prompts:

- "Score this caption from 1 to 10 on hook strength, clarity and brand fit. Explain each score, then write an improved version."
- "What questions would a skeptical buyer still have after reading this sales page?"
- "Which sentence here is weakest and why?"

Treat self-critique as a helpful second opinion, not a verdict. The model can be overly positive about its own work, or change good things unnecessarily. You still decide.

### When to restart instead

Refinement works when the draft is roughly right. Start a fresh prompt when:

- The draft is fundamentally off-target (wrong audience, wrong offer). Fix the original prompt instead.
- The conversation has become long and muddled, with conflicting instructions.
- The model keeps reverting to a style you have rejected several times.

When you restart, **update the original prompt** with what you learned, such as the missing context, the new constraint or a better example. That improved prompt becomes your reusable template.

### Worked example: a sales follow-up

A Dubai interior design studio's first AI draft of a follow-up email after a consultation is polite but generic.

1. "Too generic. Reference that the client wants a warm, family-friendly majlis and is worried about the timeline before Ramadan." The draft improves.
2. "The opening apologizes for following up. Remove that. Start with the one idea from the consultation that excited them most: the built-in low seating." Better.
3. "Add a single, low-pressure next step: a 15-minute call to review the mood board. Offer two time slots." Done.
4. "Now list any claims or promises in this email that I should double-check with the team." The model flags the timeline wording; the designer confirms it with the project manager before sending.

Four focused follow-ups turned a generic email into a specific, trustworthy one in a few minutes.

### Hands-on: a refinement drill with before/after

Use one real draft (a caption, email or ad) and run exactly three rounds, each using a different move from the toolkit:

```text
ROUND 1 - Critique then revise
Before rewriting, list the 3 biggest weaknesses of this draft for [audience] reading it on [platform].
Then fix only those 3. Keep everything else.

ROUND 2 - Surgical edit
Keep everything except [the CTA / the opening line]. Rewrite it to [specific goal].

ROUND 3 - Facts and promises check
List every factual claim, number, deadline or promise in the final version.
Mark each as: in my original notes / added by you.
```

**Before (round 0):** "We're excited to announce our new catering menu! Perfect for any occasion. Contact us today!"

**After (round 3):** "Office lunch for 20, sorted by 11:30. Our new catering menu has three set boxes (veg, chicken, mixed) delivered across Jeddah business districts. Reply with your date and headcount and we'll send a quote the same day." The round 3 check flags "the same day" as added by the AI; you confirm with the kitchen that it's true before posting.

### Refinement in modern assistants

- **Canvas-style editors** (ChatGPT canvas, Claude's artifacts and document editing, Gemini Canvas) let you highlight a sentence and ask for a change to just that part: surgical edits without regenerating everything.
- **Branching/editing a message** lets you revise your original prompt and regenerate, useful when you realize context was missing.
- When a chat gets long and muddled, ask for a summary of decisions and start fresh (see the context lesson).

### Pitfalls

- **Endless tinkering.** Set a limit of three or four rounds. If it is still not right, rethink the prompt or write that part yourself.
- **Accepting subtle drift.** Each revision can introduce new claims or change facts. Re-check facts in the final version.
- **Forgetting to save the winning prompt.** Capture it in your library.

lessons.title: Advanced techniques: step-by-step thinking, options and perspectives
lessons.body:
### Beyond one-shot requests

Once you have mastered structure and refinement, a handful of techniques can noticeably raise the quality of ideas and reasoning. None require technical knowledge.

### 1. Ask for reasoning before the answer

For strategic or analytical tasks, ask the model to think through the problem first. "Before recommending a campaign angle, analyze the audience's main motivations and objections, then recommend." Many modern models reason internally, but explicitly asking for an analysis step still helps you see and challenge the logic.

Use it for positioning decisions, choosing between offers, diagnosing why a post underperformed (with your real data), and planning a content series.

### 2. Generate many, then filter

Quantity first, then quality. "Give me 25 hook ideas. Then pick the 5 strongest for a skeptical audience and explain why." The first ideas a model produces tend to be the most predictable. Asking for more pushes it into less obvious territory, and asking it to filter gives you a first shortlist to challenge.

### 3. Constrain creatively

Constraints spark originality. Try "Write the hook as a question a customer would actually text a friend", "No adjectives in the first line", "Use a metaphor from cricket", or "Explain it as if to a grandmother in Multan".

### 4. Role-play the audience

Ask the model to become your customer and react. "You are a 32-year-old first-time buyer in Manchester with a tight budget. Read this landing page and tell me honestly what confuses you, what you doubt and what would make you click." This is a fast pre-test, not a replacement for real customer research, but it surfaces obvious gaps.

### 5. Multiple perspectives

"Give me three versions of this ad: one for a price-sensitive buyer, one for a quality-focused buyer, one for a time-poor buyer." Or ask for a debate: "Argue for and against running this campaign during exam season."

### 6. Break big tasks into chains

Instead of "Write a full launch campaign", chain smaller prompts:

1. Summarize the audience and key message (you review).
2. Generate ten campaign concepts (you pick one).
3. Draft the hero video script (you edit).
4. Create cut-downs, captions and emails from the approved script.

Each step is easier to check, and errors do not compound silently.

### 7. Ask it to ask you

"Before you write anything, ask me up to five questions that would help you write a better sales email." This is especially useful when you are not sure what context matters.

### Worked example: diagnosing a flat Reel

A Karachi streetwear brand's Reel got far fewer views than usual. The creator pastes the script, caption, posting time and simple metrics (average watch time, where viewers dropped off) and prompts:

> Analyze why this Reel may have underperformed compared to our usual posts. Consider the hook, pacing, relevance to our audience and the posting context. List three hypotheses ranked by likelihood, and for each suggest one test we could run next week. Do not assume data I have not given you.

The model suggests the hook reveals the product too late, the audio trend was already fading, and the caption lacks a reason to share. The creator tests a new hook first, which is a clear, measurable next step. The hypotheses are ideas to test, not proven causes.

### Reasoning models and research modes: when to switch them on

- **Thinking/reasoning modes** (available in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot, with different names) spend more time working through a problem. Use them for positioning decisions, diagnosing underperformance with real data, and planning a content series or sales sequence. Don't bother for captions and subject lines.
- **Deep research** is the right tool when the thinking needs **current external facts**: competitor positioning, a market's buying cycle, a prospect's recent news.
- You still need to **show your data** and **challenge the logic**. A longer answer is not automatically a better one.

### Hands-on: a strategy prompt with hypotheses

```text
Context: [brand, audience, goal]. Data: [paste real numbers: reach, watch time, clicks, conversions for the last 8 posts].
Task: Analyze why [the last 3 posts] underperformed compared with our usual posts.
Give 3 hypotheses ranked by likelihood, the evidence for each from my data only,
and one cheap test per hypothesis we could run next week.
Do not assume data I haven't given you. If the data can't distinguish between hypotheses, say so.
```

**Before:** "Why are my posts doing badly?" returns generic advice about posting times and hashtags.

lessons.title: Context packs: projects, files and memory for content and sales
lessons.body:
### Context engineering for content and sales

"Context engineering" means deliberately deciding **what the model sees** before it writes: which instructions, facts, examples and files. For content and sales work, most quality problems are context problems. The fix is a reusable **context pack** stored where your assistant can use it.

### What goes in a context pack

| Component | Contents | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Brand voice guide** | Personality (this, not that), language rules, love/ban words | Consistent voice |
| **Offer sheet** | Products/services, prices, what's included, guarantees (real ones only), terms | Stops invented facts |
| **Approved claims and proof** | Claims legal has approved, case study results with permission, testimonials with consent | Proof without fabrication |
| **Customer language** | Verbatim pains, desires and objections from reviews, calls and DMs (anonymized) | Copy that sounds like buyers |
| **Example bank** | Best-performing posts, emails and scripts | Tone transfer |
| **Do-not list** | Claims needing sign-off, sensitive topics, competitor rules, disclosure requirements | Guardrails |

Keep each file short and dated. One page per component beats one 40-page document.

### Where to store it (2026)

- **ChatGPT Projects** (instructions + files, optional project-only memory) or a **custom GPT** for a repeatable task you share with a team.
- **Claude Projects** (project instructions + project knowledge files).
- **Gemini Gems** (saved instructions and files) and **Gemini Notebook** when you want answers grounded only in your sources.
- **Microsoft 365 Copilot**: Copilot Notebooks, or reference files in SharePoint/OneDrive that Copilot can access.
- **Notion AI**: a brand hub page that Notion AI can read across your workspace.

Business plans matter here: client and sales material belongs in a work-approved workspace.

### Writing project instructions that use the pack

```text
You write marketing and sales content for [brand].
Always read and follow: Voice guide.pdf, Offer sheet.pdf, Approved claims.pdf, Do-not list.pdf.
Use Customer language.pdf for phrasing and Example bank.pdf for tone and structure (don't copy phrases).
If a fact isn't in these files, write [CHECK] instead of guessing.
Every output ends with:
- "Claims used:" each claim and which file it came from
- "Disclosure:" any #ad / paid label / AI label needed
```

### Per-task context: the three lines that still matter

Even with a pack, add three lines per task: **the goal**, **the specific audience segment**, and **what's different this time** (a new offer, a season, a competitor move). The pack supplies the stable truth; these lines supply the moment.

### Memory: helpful for you, risky for clients

Assistant memory is great for **your** preferences (format, spelling, how you like options presented). Keep client and prospect details **out of global memory**; keep them in the project. Review memory monthly.

### Worked example (illustrative)

A B2B agency in Riyadh writes content and sales emails for a logistics software client. Before: every writer pasted different, sometimes outdated, facts; one email quoted last year's pricing. After: a Claude Project with six one-page files and the instructions above. Outputs end with "Claims used" mapped to files, so the account lead can check them in a minute. When the client updates pricing, one file changes and every future draft is correct.

### Hands-on: build your context pack in 45 minutes

1. Create the six files (start rough; one page each).
2. Create a project/GPT/Gem and paste the instructions template.
3. Upload the files; set a calendar reminder to review them quarterly.
4. Test with three real tasks (a post, a sales email, an ad).

**Before (plain chat):** "Write a cold email to a logistics manager about our route software" produces a generic email claiming "cut costs by 30%".

**After (with the pack):** an email using a customer's own phrase ("my drivers call me from the road all day"), one approved result with the client's permission, the correct price tier, no invented percentages, and a "Claims used" list you verify in seconds.

### Pitfalls

- One enormous, undated document instead of short, dated files.
- Outdated offer sheets (the most common source of wrong prices).
- Mixing several clients' packs in one project.
- Assuming the model read every file; ask for "Claims used" to see what it relied on.

### How to measure success

Track first-draft acceptance rate and the number of factual corrections per draft before and after the pack. Both should improve within two weeks.

lessons.body:
### Why templates

Once you find a prompt that works, turn it into a **template** with [placeholders]. Templates make quality repeatable, save time and let teammates or freelancers produce consistent work. Paste your brand voice guide (Module 5) or use your context pack (Module 2) with any template for best results.

### Template 1: Hook generator

> You are a short-form video strategist for [niche] creators.
> Audience: [who, age, location, main desire, main frustration].
> Video topic: [topic]. Key point of the video: [one sentence].
> Write 15 opening hooks (first 1–2 seconds, spoken, under 12 words each).
> Use a mix of these angles: curiosity gap, bold contrarian statement, relatable pain, specific result, question, "mistake" framing.
> Avoid clickbait that the video does not deliver on. No false claims.
> Format: numbered list, with the angle in brackets after each.

**Why it works:** audience plus a single key point keeps hooks relevant; named angles force variety; the honesty rule prevents misleading hooks that hurt retention and trust.

### Template 2: Caption writer

> Write [number] [platform] captions for this post: [describe the visual/video].
> Goal: [saves / comments / DMs / link clicks / sales].
> Voice: [3 adjectives + 1 example caption].
> Structure: hook line that works alone before the "more" cut-off; [1–3] short body lines with one specific detail; CTA aligned to the goal.
> Constraints: under [X] words; [language/variety]; banned words: [list]; [#ad / paid partnership label if sponsored].
> Format: numbered, with a one-line note on why each should achieve the goal.

### Template 3: Short-form video script

> Write a [length]-second [platform] script about [topic] for [audience].
> Structure:
> 0–3s: hook (spoken + on-screen text)
> 3–[X]s: [2–3] beats delivering the key point with one example
> Final 5s: CTA ([follow / comment keyword / link in bio])
> Constraints: voiceover under [word count] words (about 2.5 words per second is a comfortable pace); simple spoken language; one pattern interrupt midway.
> Format: table with columns Time | Visual | Voiceover | On-screen text.

### Template 4: Content repurposer

> Here is [a transcript / blog / podcast summary]: [paste].
> Extract the [3–5] most useful, specific ideas, using the speaker's own phrasing where possible.
> For each, create: one [platform] post, one carousel outline (6–8 slides), one short-video hook.
> Do not add facts or advice that are not in the source. Mark anything that needs a visual with [VISUAL].

### Template 5: Content calendar

> Create a [2/4]-week content calendar for [brand] on [platforms].
> Content pillars: [3–5 pillars with a short description].
> Key dates: [launches, holidays such as Ramadan, Eid, Diwali, Black Friday or back to school].
> Posting frequency: [per platform].
> Format: table with columns Date, Platform, Pillar, Format, Hook, CTA.
> Balance pillars and do not schedule promotional posts back to back.

### Worked example: filling in the hook template

A Lahore-based personal finance creator fills in Template 1: audience "salaried professionals 24–35 in Pakistan who feel they never save", topic "the 50/30/20 budget adapted for high inflation", key point "percentages matter less than automating savings on payday".

Selected outputs:

- (Contrarian) "The 50/30/20 rule doesn't work in Pakistan. Here's what does."
- (Relatable pain) "Salary comes on the 1st, gone by the 20th?"
- (Mistake) "You're saving what's left. That's the mistake."

She picks the contrarian hook, checks that the video actually explains the adapted method, and films it. Note what the template prevented: hooks promising "guaranteed returns", which would be misleading and potentially a regulatory problem for financial content.

### Hands-on: turn a template into a saved tool

A template is most useful when it's one click away. Pick the template you'll use most and save it as:

- a **custom GPT** or a **Gemini Gem** (instructions = the template with a note to ask for the placeholders), or
- a **saved prompt / project instruction** in Claude or ChatGPT, or
- a **Notion page** with the template that Notion AI can run on selected text.

```text
Instructions for a "Hook Generator" GPT/Gem
You generate short-form video hooks for [brand/niche].
First ask me for: the audience, the video topic and the one key point.
Then write 15 hooks under 12 words each across these angles: curiosity, contrarian, pain, result, question, mistake.
Never promise what the video doesn't deliver; no guaranteed results, no fake scarcity.
Return a numbered list with the angle in brackets, then recommend the 3 strongest for a skeptical viewer and why.
```

**Before:** everyone on the team writes hooks differently, and quality depends on who's on shift.

**After:** a shared Hook Generator that asks for the three inputs, enforces honesty rules and returns tagged options, so a new freelancer produces on-brand hooks on day one.

### Template quality check

Before you share a template, test it on three different topics and check: Are placeholders obvious? Does it block the risky outputs (claims, fake urgency)? Does the format fit where the output goes? Does it still work when someone else fills it in?

### Adapting templates

- **Swap angles** for your niche. B2B might use "cost of inaction" or "peer benchmark".
- **Add platform specifics** such as character limits, hashtag norms and whether captions are read at all.
- **Localize:** specify language variety and cultural references explicitly.

lessons.title: Long-form content with prompt chains: articles, newsletters, case studies and landing pages
lessons.body:
### Long-form needs a chain, not a prompt

Blog posts, newsletters, case studies and landing pages are too long and too important for a single prompt. One-shot long-form output is where generic filler, invented facts and structural drift appear. The professional approach is a **prompt chain**: small steps with a human checkpoint between each.

### The five-step long-form chain

```text
STEP 1 - Angle and brief
Topic: [topic]. Audience: [segment]. Goal: [subscribe / book / buy / understand].
Using our context pack, propose 5 angles, each with a working title, the reader's question it answers,
and why it's different from what competitors publish. Don't write the piece.
```

You choose the angle.

```text
STEP 2 - Outline
Create an outline for the chosen angle: H2/H3 headings, one line per section on its purpose,
where a customer quote, example or data point belongs ([PROOF] placeholders), and the CTA.
Target length: [X] words.
```

You edit the outline (this is the highest-leverage edit you'll make).

```text
STEP 3 - Section drafts
Draft section [N] only, about [X] words, from my notes: [paste].
Use only facts in my notes and the context pack; write [CHECK] otherwise. Keep our voice.
```

Repeat per section, adding your own examples as you go.

```text
STEP 4 - Edit passes (run separately)
a) Voice pass: flag sentences that break our voice guide or sound generic; suggest fixes.
b) Cut pass: cut 20% without losing any fact, example or step.
c) Claims pass: list every factual claim, number and promise with its source (my notes / context pack / none).
```

```text
STEP 5 - Packaging
Write 5 headline options, a 150-character meta description, an email subject line + preview text,
and 3 social posts that promote the piece without repeating its opening.
```

### Format-specific tips

| Format | What makes it work | Prompt addition |
|---|---|---|
| **Newsletter** | One idea, personal voice, one link | "One idea only; first line personal; one CTA" |
| **Case study** | Real customer, real numbers, their words | "Use only the interview notes; quote the customer; approved results only" |
| **Landing page** | One offer, objections answered, proof near CTA | "Sections: hero, problem, how it works, proof, FAQ from real objections, CTA" |
| **Blog / SEO article** | Answers the searcher's question fully, with experience | "Start with the direct answer; add our process and examples" |

### Worked example (illustrative)

A cybersecurity consultancy in Dubai wants a case study about helping a logistics client pass an audit. Step 1 proposes five angles; the team picks "What we fixed in the first 30 days". The outline puts the client's quote near the top and places [PROOF] where audit results go. Section drafts use only the interview notes. The claims pass flags one sentence ("reduced risk by 60%") as having no source; the team replaces it with the client-approved outcome (passed the audit on first attempt). The client approves the final draft before publishing.

### Hands-on: run the chain on one piece this week

Pick a newsletter, case study or landing page you need. Run steps 1 to 5 in one chat inside your context-pack project, editing at each checkpoint.

**Before (one prompt):** "Write a 1,200-word blog post about reducing employee turnover" produces a list of 10 generic tips ("offer competitive salaries", "foster a positive culture") and two invented statistics.

**After (chain):** an article built around one angle ("Exit interviews are too late: the 3 stay conversations we run instead"), your real process and a client example, [CHECK] tags replaced with verified facts, a clean claims list, and a promotion kit.

### Using document editors and agents for long-form

Canvas-style editors (ChatGPT canvas, Claude's document editing, Gemini Canvas) and in-app assistants (Copilot in Word, Gemini in Docs, Notion AI) make the chain easier: you can keep the outline and draft in one document, highlight a single section to redraft, and run the edit passes on selected text. Agent modes can also gather inputs for you, for example pulling the interview notes, the approved results and last quarter's case studies from a shared drive into one working document. Keep the checkpoints human: an agent can assemble materials, but you approve the angle, the outline and every claim.

### Pitfalls

- Skipping the outline edit; structure problems are expensive to fix later.
- Letting sections add facts not in your notes.
- Running all edit passes in one prompt (they interfere); run them separately.
- Publishing case studies or testimonials without the customer's approval.

### How to measure success

For each long-form piece, track time to publish, number of factual corrections found in review, and the piece's goal metric (subscribers, bookings, time on page, assisted conversions).

lessons.title: Prospect research and outreach prompts
lessons.body:
### Research, insight, message

Good outreach follows a simple chain: **research** (what's true about this company now) leads to an **insight** (why they might care, now) leads to a **message** (short, specific, one easy ask). AI speeds up all three, but the chain breaks if the research is wrong, the insight is generic, or the message is creepy.

### Step 1: account research (public, professional information only)

Use web search, deep research or Perplexity for a one-page account brief:

```text
Company: [name], [country/city], [website].
Using public sources from the last 12 months, give me:
1. What they do, who they sell to, and how they describe themselves (quote their site)
2. Recent news: launches, expansion, hiring, funding, leadership changes (with links and dates)
3. Likely priorities or pains relevant to [what we sell], labeled as hypotheses
4. Two or three specific, non-obvious conversation openers based on the above
Mark anything single-sourced. Company and professional information only.
```

Open the two or three links you'll mention. A wrong "congratulations on your expansion" ends the conversation.

### Step 2: from research to insight

```text
Given this account brief and our context pack (offer sheet, approved proof, customer language),
what is the ONE most relevant reason this company might care about [our offer] now?
Give the reason, the evidence from the brief, the proof point we can use, and a one-line hook.
If there's no strong reason, say so; we'll deprioritize this account.
```

"No strong reason, deprioritize" is a feature: it stops you sending weak outreach.

### Step 3: the message

```text
Write a [LinkedIn message / email] to [role] at [company].
Opening: the insight, specific to them (not about us).
Middle: one sentence on what we do + one approved proof point.
Ask: one low-friction question (not a meeting request in the first message).
Rules: under [80] words; no flattery clichés; no fake familiarity; no invented mutual connections,
results or urgency; plain text; include our opt-out line for email.
Give 2 versions with different openings.
```

### Personalization tiers

| Tier | When | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| **1:1** | Top accounts | Full research, insight and hand-edited message |
| **Segment** | Similar companies (e.g. clinics opening second branches in Riyadh) | One insight per segment, light personalization |
| **Trigger-based** | A public event (new location, new role, funding) | Short message tied to the trigger |

Don't fake 1:1 personalization at scale; recipients notice.

### Compliance essentials

Outreach rules differ by country. Examples: in the **US**, CAN-SPAM requires honest headers and subject lines, a physical address and a working opt-out for commercial email; in the **UK and EU**, GDPR and (in the UK) PECR govern using personal data and sending electronic marketing, with stricter rules for individuals and sole traders; the **UAE and Saudi Arabia** have their own data-protection laws. Research only professional information, honor opt-outs, and follow your company's policy. For deliverability and compliance in depth, see [AI for Sales Teams](/learn/ai-for-sales-teams).

### Worked example (illustrative)

Ayesha sells scheduling software to clinics from Karachi into the Gulf. For a Riyadh dental group, account research finds a public announcement of a second branch opening next quarter (confirmed on the group's own site). The insight: scheduling across two branches is the pain her customers describe most ("patients booked at the wrong branch"). Her 70-word LinkedIn message opens with the second branch, cites one approved result from a similar clinic group, and asks one question: "How are you planning to handle bookings across both branches?" She gets a reply asking for a short demo.

### Hands-on: three accounts in 45 minutes

1. Pick three real target accounts.
2. Run the account research prompt; open and confirm the facts you'll mention.
3. Run the insight prompt; drop any account with "no strong reason".
4. Draft two message versions each; edit the first line by hand.

**Before:** "Hi [Name], I hope you're well! I came across your company and was impressed. We help businesses like yours grow. Do you have 30 minutes this week?"

**After:** "Saw [Company] is opening a second branch in [district] next quarter. Clinic groups we work with say double-bookings across branches are the first headache. One group cut them sharply after moving to a shared schedule [approved proof]. How are you planning to handle bookings across both sites?"

### Pitfalls

- Mentioning "news" you didn't verify.
- Researching personal lives (family, holidays, personal social accounts).
- Invented mutual connections, results or deadlines.
- Automating sends of AI-written messages without review.

### How to measure success

Track reply rate and positive-reply rate per tier and per insight type, not just volume sent. Fewer, better messages usually win.

lessons.title: Call prep, rehearsal and post-call follow-up
lessons.body:
### Better calls start with better questions

Discovery calls decide deals. AI can help you prepare in 15 minutes, rehearse the hard moments, and turn the call into accurate notes and next steps. What it can't do is listen for you: the call itself is where your judgment matters most.

### The 15-minute call-prep pack

```text
1. CALL BRIEF
I have a [30]-minute discovery call with [role] at [company] about [topic].
From this account brief and CRM notes (anonymized where needed): [paste]
Give me: what we know, what we don't know, the 3 most likely priorities (as hypotheses),
and the single outcome I should aim for by the end of the call.
```

```text
2. QUESTION BANK
Write 12 discovery questions in 4 groups: situation, problem, impact, decision process.
Open-ended, one question at a time, no leading questions, plain language.
Mark the 5 I must ask if time runs short.
```

```text
3. OBJECTION PREVIEW
List the 5 objections this buyer is most likely to raise, with an honest 2-sentence response
for each using only our offer sheet and approved proof. Mark any response that needs data I haven't given you.
```

```text
4. ROLE-PLAY (voice mode)
You are [role] at a [company type]. You're busy and skeptical; you've been burned by a similar tool before.
I'm running discovery for [offer]. Answer realistically, push back twice, and don't volunteer information unless I ask good questions.
After 10 minutes, stop and score my questions: which uncovered real information, which were leading, what I missed.
```

### During the call

- Use your question bank as a guide, not a script.
- Take rough notes on **their words** for pains and priorities; you'll reuse them.
- If you use meeting recording or transcription, tell participants and follow your company policy and local law.

### After the call: notes to next steps

```text
Here are my notes / the transcript from a discovery call with [company]: [paste].
Produce:
1. Their top 3 priorities in their own words (quote them)
2. Current situation and what they've tried
3. Impact if nothing changes (only what they said)
4. Decision process: who's involved, timeline, budget signals (write "Unknown" if not stated)
5. Agreed next step with date and owner
6. CRM summary in 5 lines
7. A follow-up email draft (under 150 words) reflecting their words, with one next step and two time options
Finally: list any promise, number or claim in the email that I should confirm before sending.
```

### Worked example (illustrative)

James sells HR software to mid-size companies in the UK. Before a call with a retail chain's HR director, he runs the prep pack. The question bank includes "Walk me through what happens when a store manager needs cover for a sick shift." The voice role-play (with the AI playing a skeptical HR director) shows he leads with product features too early; he moves them to the end. On the call, the director says, "Our managers spend Sunday nights on WhatsApp finding cover." The post-call prompt puts that quote at the top of the follow-up, and the "confirm" list flags an implementation timeline he mentioned loosely; he checks it with his implementation team before sending.

### Hands-on: prep your next real call

Run prompts 1 to 3 the day before, prompt 4 for 10 minutes in voice mode, and the post-call prompt within an hour of the call.

**Before:** you arrive with the prospect's website open and a mental list of product features.

**After:** you arrive with the outcome you want, five must-ask questions, honest answers to likely objections, one rehearsal behind you, and a follow-up that goes out within the hour quoting the buyer's own words.

### Using connected assistants and CRM AI

If your assistant is connected to your email, calendar or CRM (where your organization allows), it can assemble the call brief for you: past emails with the account, the last meeting's notes and open opportunities. Many CRMs and meeting tools now include their own AI call summaries. Treat these like any other draft: check that quotes are accurate, that "decisions" were really agreed, and that nothing sensitive is written into shared records. Keep a human review between any AI summary and the CRM fields your forecast depends on.

### Pitfalls

- Reading questions like a survey; listen and follow up.
- Treating the role-play as a real buyer's opinion; it's practice.
- Letting the AI fill "Unknown" fields in your CRM with guesses.
- Recording without consent.

### How to measure success

Track the share of calls that end with a concrete next step, how quickly follow-ups go out, and stage conversion from discovery to proposal.

lessons.body:
### Revenue copy needs guardrails

Sales and advertising copy has direct consequences: money, contracts and regulatory exposure. So templates in this lesson share two rules:

1. **Supply the facts** (offer, price, deadline, proof) explicitly.
2. **Forbid invention:** "Do not invent testimonials, results, statistics, discounts or deadlines. Use [PLACEHOLDER] where proof would help."

### Template 6: Ad copy variations

> You are a performance copywriter for [platform] ads.
> Product/offer: [what, price, key benefit, guarantee if real].
> Audience: [segment, main pain, main desire, main objection].
> Write [8] ad variations using these angles: pain, dream outcome, objection-handling, social proof (use only this approved proof: [paste]), direct offer.
> For each: primary text (under [X] words), headline (under [X] characters), description (under [X] characters).
> Constraints: comply with [platform] ad policies; no personal-attribute targeting language (e.g. "Are you overweight?"); no exaggerated or absolute claims.
> Format: table.

Note the personal-attributes rule: major ad platforms restrict copy that implies you know a person's health, finances, religion or other sensitive characteristics.

### Template 7: Email sequence

> Write a [3]-email sequence for [segment: e.g. people who downloaded our free guide on X].
> Goal: [book a call / buy / start trial].
> Facts: [offer, price, deadline, what's included].
> Email 1: deliver value related to the guide, soft mention of offer.
> Email 2: address the top objection [objection] with a real example [paste or placeholder].
> Email 3: clear offer, honest deadline, simple CTA.
> Each: subject line + preview text (under 90 characters), body under [150] words, one CTA.
> Voice: [paste guide]. Include an unsubscribe reminder line.

### Template 8: Cold outreach (B2B or collaborations)

> Draft a short, personalized outreach message to [role] at [company type] via [email/LinkedIn/Instagram DM].
> What I know about them (public info only): [paste].
> What I offer: [one sentence]. Relevant proof: [one real result or client, if permitted].
> Rules: under [90] words; open with something specific to them, not about me; one clear, low-friction ask; no flattery clichés; no fake familiarity.

### Template 9: Post-call follow-up

> Here are my notes from a discovery call with [prospect]: [paste notes, remove sensitive personal data].
> Write a follow-up email that:
> 1. Thanks them and reflects their top two goals in their own words.
> 2. Summarizes what we agreed and any open questions.
> 3. Proposes one next step with two time options.
> Tone: [warm, professional, confident]. Under [150] words.
> Finally, list any promises or figures in the email I should confirm before sending.

### Template 10: Objection handler

> Our prospects often say: "[objection]".
> Our honest answer, in facts: [facts].
> Write 3 ways to respond: one for a DM, one for a sales call (spoken), one for a FAQ page. Acknowledge the concern first. Do not pressure or dismiss.

### Worked example: follow-up for an influencer collaboration

Zara, a UAE-based creator manager, just had a call with a skincare brand about a paid campaign. Her notes cover the brand's goal (awareness in KSA and UAE), budget range, deliverables discussed (three Reels, two story sets), their worry (previous creator content felt "too ad-like"), and next steps (Zara to send a proposal).

Using Template 9, the draft reflects their goals, reassures them about native-feeling content, and proposes a proposal review call. The "promises to confirm" list flags that the draft mentioned "guaranteed reach", which Zara never promised. She removes it. She also adds a line confirming that all sponsored content will carry clear disclosure in line with platform tools and local advertising rules.

### Hands-on: run Template 9 on a real call and compare

Take notes from your last sales or partnership call and run Template 9 (post-call follow-up) twice: once as a bare request ("write a follow-up email") and once with the full template.

**Before (bare request):** "Thank you for your time today! It was great learning about your business. As discussed, our solution can help you achieve your goals. Let me know if you have any questions!"

**After (Template 9):** an email that opens with the prospect's two goals in their own words, summarizes what was agreed, proposes one next step with two time options, and ends with a "confirm before sending" list that flags a delivery date you mentioned casually.

### Where these templates live

Store Templates 6 to 10 in your sales project alongside your context pack (offer sheet, approved proof, objection library), or as a shared custom GPT/Gem for the team. If your CRM offers built-in AI (for example Salesforce, HubSpot or Microsoft Dynamics features enabled by your admin), you can run similar prompts where the customer data already lives, which is usually safer than pasting CRM exports into a general assistant.

### Ad copy: where to go deeper

Template 6 covers copy. For AI campaign types, bidding, creative testing at scale and measurement, see [AI-Powered Performance Marketing](/learn/ai-performance-marketing).

### Pitfalls

- **Pasting raw CRM exports.** Anonymize or trim to what the email needs.
- **Over-personalization.** Referencing a prospect's family photos from Instagram is creepy, not clever.
- **Deadlines that are not real.** "Offer ends tonight" must be true.
- **Automating send.** Draft with AI; send after human review, especially for new templates.

Content grabs attention. But it's emails, ads and follow-ups that turn attention into revenue. Let's look at how to prompt for them.

The golden rule for sales prompts is simple. Give the model the facts it can't guess, and forbid it from inventing anything else. That means your real offer, your real price, your real deadline, and genuine proof you have permission to use.

For ad copy, ask for variations built on different angles: the pain, the dream outcome, social proof, and a direct offer. Ask for headlines within the platform's character limits, and then check those limits yourself, because models count tokens, not letters.

For sales emails, give the context of the relationship. Is this a cold prospect, a warm lead who downloaded a guide, or someone who went quiet after a proposal? Each needs a different tone and a different next step.

For follow-ups after a call, paste your own notes and ask the model to reference the prospect's specific goals, confirm next steps, and offer one easy action, like a fifteen-minute call with two time options.

And always add a line like this: do not invent testimonials, results, discounts or deadlines. If proof would help, insert a placeholder.

Why? Because false urgency, fake reviews and made-up results can break consumer-protection and advertising rules in the UK, the US, the Gulf and beyond. And more importantly, they break trust.

Use the templates in this lesson as your starting point, then adapt them to your voice.

lessons.title: Proposals, objection handling and RFP answers
lessons.body:
### Proposals win when they mirror the buyer

A proposal is a decision document. The best ones mirror the buyer's own words back to them, make the choice easy, and contain nothing you can't deliver. AI can assemble a strong first draft in minutes from your discovery notes and context pack, but pricing, scope and commitments are yours to decide.

### The proposal chain

```text
STEP 1 - Structure from discovery
From these discovery notes [paste] and our context pack, outline a proposal:
1. Their situation and goals (in their words)
2. What success looks like (their measures)
3. Our recommended approach (phases)
4. Options (good / better / best) with what's included
5. Timeline and responsibilities (ours and theirs)
6. Investment [PRICING - I'll supply]
7. Proof (approved case studies only)
8. Next steps
Mark anything you'd need from me as [DECIDE].
```

```text
STEP 2 - Draft sections
Draft sections 1-3 using only the notes and context pack. Quote the buyer where possible.
No promises about results; describe what we'll do, not guarantees.
```

```text
STEP 3 - Options table
Create a good/better/best table from this scope and pricing [paste], showing what's included,
timeline and who each option suits. Don't change any price or scope.
```

```text
STEP 4 - Buyer's-eye review
Read this proposal as [the buyer's CFO / procurement lead]. What's unclear, what's missing,
what would you push back on, and what could be misread as a guarantee?
```

### An objection library, not one-off replies

Most teams hear the same ten objections. Build a library once and reuse it:

```text
For each objection below, write:
- What's usually behind it (the real concern)
- An honest response in 2-3 sentences using only our facts and approved proof
- A question to ask back
- A version for email, a version to say on a call
Objections: "too expensive", "we're happy with our current provider", "not the right time",
"we need to involve IT", "can you just send some information?"
Do not pressure, dismiss or invent proof.
```

Review the library with your best salesperson, keep it in your sales project, and add real phrasings as you hear them.

### RFP and questionnaire answers

For requests for proposal and security or supplier questionnaires, a source-grounded setup works best: upload approved past answers, policies and product documentation to a project or Gemini Notebook and ask it to draft answers **only from those sources, citing the document**. Anything without a source gets flagged for a subject-matter expert. Never let AI invent compliance statements or certifications.

### Worked example (illustrative)

Farah runs a small events agency in Dubai. After discovery with a tech company planning a regional sales kickoff, she runs the proposal chain. The draft quotes the client's goal ("a kickoff people actually talk about in March, not just attend"), offers three packages she priced herself, and the buyer's-eye review (as the client's procurement lead) flags that "we'll ensure 100% attendee satisfaction" reads like a guarantee. She replaces it with what the agency will do (pre-event survey, live feedback, post-event report). She wins the project on the "better" option.

### Hands-on: one proposal and five objections

1. Run the four-step chain on a real or recent opportunity.
2. Build the objection library for your five most common objections.
3. Save both in your sales project.

**Before:** a proposal reused from a previous client, with their name replaced (and one mention missed), generic benefits and a single take-it-or-leave-it price.

**After:** a proposal that opens with this buyer's goals in their words, offers three clear options, lists both parties' responsibilities, uses only approved proof, and has survived a skeptical CFO review.

### A proposal checklist before sending

- [ ] The first page is about their goals, in their words, not our history.
- [ ] Every option lists what's included, timeline and who it suits; prices match the price list exactly.
- [ ] Both parties' responsibilities and assumptions are stated.
- [ ] No sentence reads as a guarantee of results.
- [ ] Every case study and logo is approved for use.
- [ ] No other client's name or details anywhere (search the document).
- [ ] The next step has a date and an owner.

### Pitfalls

- Letting AI set or "optimize" pricing and scope.
- Guarantees disguised as enthusiasm ("we'll double your leads").
- Proof from case studies you don't have permission to share.
- Copy-pasting old proposals with the wrong client's details.

The buyer couldn't see their own problem in it. In this lecture you'll learn a four step proposal chain that mirrors the buyer's words, offers clear options and survives a skeptical review, plus how to build an objection library once and use it forever, and how to draft RFP answers safely. You'll see a Dubai events agency win a project, and watch me run a buyer's eye review that catches an accidental guarantee.

They offer one price, take it or leave it, which turns the decision into yes or no instead of which one. And they contain accidental guarantees, enthusiastic lines like we'll double your leads, that create legal risk and make careful buyers nervous. AI can make all three problems worse, by producing polished, generic proposals quickly. Used well, it fixes all three.

lessons.title: Building a brand voice guide for AI
lessons.body:
### Why a voice guide

Without a voice guide, every prompt reinvents your tone and the output drifts towards generic AI style. A concise, AI-ready **brand voice guide** pasted at the top of prompts (or saved in a tool's project or custom-instructions feature) makes outputs consistent across people, platforms and months.

### What to include (one page)

1. **Brand in one sentence:** who you serve and how you are different.
2. **Audience snapshot:** who they are, the words they use, what they care about.
3. **Personality:** three to four traits, each with "this, not that". For example: *Warm, not gushing. Confident, not arrogant. Playful, not silly.*
4. **Language rules:** British or American spelling, Arabic dialect, Urdu or Roman Urdu use, emoji policy, contractions, sentence length.
5. **Vocabulary:** words and phrases you love; words you ban.
6. **Formatting habits:** line breaks, lists, hashtags, sign-offs.
7. **Examples:** three to five real pieces that nail the voice, labeled by type.
8. **Guardrails:** claims you never make, topics you avoid, required disclosures.

### Example: a compact voice guide

> **Brand:** Chai & Charts, a personal finance creator helping young Pakistani professionals build savings without guilt.
> **Audience:** 22–35, salaried, urban, bilingual; phrases they use: "salary khatam", "side hustle", "committee".
> **Personality:** Friendly, not preachy. Honest, not alarmist. Practical, not theoretical.
> **Language:** Simple English with light Roman Urdu; short sentences; no jargon without a plain explanation; max two emojis.
> **Love:** "small wins", "boring money is good money", "here's the math".
> **Ban:** "financial freedom guaranteed", "get rich", "elevate", "unlock", "hustle harder".
> **Guardrails:** Never recommend specific stocks, funds or crypto; never promise returns; always say "not financial advice" on investment topics; disclose sponsorships with #ad and the platform's paid partnership label.
> **Examples:** [3 labeled captions]

### Using it in prompts

- **Paste on top:** "Follow this brand voice guide strictly: [guide]. Now: [task]."
- **Project or custom instructions:** many assistants let you store instructions for a project so you do not have to paste every time. Check what data the feature stores.
- **Voice check prompt:** "Review this draft against our voice guide. List each place it breaks the guide, then provide a corrected version."

### Building the guide with AI

You can use AI to draft the guide from your own content:

> Here are 10 of my best-performing posts: [paste]. Analyze the voice: personality traits, sentence patterns, vocabulary, formatting, and what I never do. Draft a one-page brand voice guide using the structure: Brand, Audience, Personality (this, not that), Language rules, Love words, Ban words, Formatting, Guardrails.

Then **edit it yourself**. The model describes patterns; only you know which are intentional and which are bad habits.

### Hands-on: draft, test and store your voice guide

**1. Draft from your best work**

```text
Here are 10 of our best-performing pieces (posts, emails, scripts): [paste].
Analyze the voice: personality traits, sentence patterns, vocabulary, formatting, and what we never do.
Draft a one-page voice guide: Brand, Audience (with their phrases), Personality (this, not that),
Language rules, Love words, Ban words, Formatting, Guardrails (claims, topics, disclosure).
Mark anything you're unsure is intentional with [CONFIRM].
```

**2. Blind test**

Generate five pieces with the guide, mix them with five real pieces, and ask a colleague (or the client) to pick which are human-written. If they can easily spot the AI ones, note what gave them away and add it to the guide.

**3. Store it where it's always applied**

Put the guide in your project instructions or files (ChatGPT/Claude Projects), a Gem or custom GPT, a Copilot Notebook, or the brand hub page Notion AI reads. Claude's **custom styles** can also be created from writing samples, and ChatGPT's custom instructions can carry your personal voice; keep **brand** voices in their projects, and your **personal** voice in your own settings.

**Before:** "Friendly, authentic, innovative" at the top of a prompt, and drafts full of exclamation marks and "elevate".

**After:** a one-page guide with this-not-that traits, love/ban lists and three labeled examples; the blind test shows colleagues can no longer reliably spot which captions were AI-drafted after human editing.

### Multiple voices

Agencies and creators with several brands should keep one guide per brand or client, clearly named, and never mix them in the same chat. Test a guide by generating five pieces and asking a colleague or the client, "Does this sound like us?"

### Pitfalls

- **Adjective soup:** "authentic, innovative, bold, human" means nothing without examples.
- **Guides that are too long:** keep the core to about a page; the model and your team need to absorb it.
- **Set and forget:** update when your positioning changes or you notice recurring edits.

Different people on your team describe the voice differently, so the brand sounds like three brands. And over months, it wanders. A concise guide, stored where the AI always sees it, makes outputs consistent across people, platforms and time. And consistency is what makes a brand recognizable. Because a single adjective gives the model a direction, but not a limit. Warm could mean anything up to effusive. Warm, not gushing tells it exactly where to stop. It's like tuning a radio: the adjective gets you to the right station, and the not that gets rid of the static. Three or four of these pairs capture more than a paragraph of adjectives.

lessons.title: Evaluating outputs and fact-checking before you publish
lessons.body:
### Quality is a process, not a feeling

"It looks good" is not an evaluation. Professionals use a consistent checklist so quality does not depend on mood or deadline pressure. This lesson gives you a practical evaluation rubric and a fact-checking routine for AI-assisted content.

### The CLEAR rubric

Score each piece from 1 to 5 on:

- **C: Correct.** Are facts, numbers, names, prices, dates and claims verified?
- **L: Legal and compliant.** Disclosures (#ad, paid partnership, AI labels where required), platform ad policies, no misleading claims, no infringing content.
- **E: Engaging.** Does the hook earn attention? Is there a specific detail or story?
- **A: Audience fit.** Right language, culture, sophistication and platform norms?
- **R: Recognisably us.** Does it match the voice guide and sound human, not generic?

Anything scoring 1 or 2 on C or L does not ship, regardless of how engaging it is.

### Fact-checking routine

1. **Extract claims.** Ask the model: "List every factual claim in this text as a bullet list." That makes checking faster.
2. **Categorize.** Brand facts (price, ingredients, dates) are checked against the client brief or product page. External facts (market data, news, rules) are checked against primary sources: the regulator, the official report or the platform's help center.
3. **Verify or cut.** If you cannot verify within reasonable time, rewrite qualitatively or remove.
4. **Watch for subtle drift.** AI may turn "up to 40% off selected items" into "40% off everything". Compare offer wording word for word.
5. **Record sources** for sponsored and regulated content.

### Using AI to help evaluate

AI can support, but not replace, your evaluation:

- "Evaluate this caption against the CLEAR rubric and our voice guide. Be critical and specific."
- "Identify any statements that could be seen as misleading to a consumer."
- "Which parts of this would a native Gulf Arabic speaker find unnatural?" This is a pointer only; confirm with a native speaker.

Be aware that models can be agreeable and may rate their own work generously. Use a fresh chat for evaluation, and ask for weaknesses specifically.

### A/B testing: letting the audience decide

For hooks, subject lines and ads, the best evaluator is your audience. Use AI to generate distinct variants, not near-duplicates, then test them with platform A/B tools or by posting variants over time. Keep a simple log: variant, angle, result. Feed winners back into your examples.

### Hands-on: a CLEAR review routine in a fresh chat

Run evaluation in a **fresh chat** (or a separate "Reviewer" project) so the model isn't grading its own conversation:

```text
You are a strict reviewer. Evaluate the draft below against:
- Our voice guide (attached)
- The CLEAR rubric: Correct, Legal/compliant, Engaging, Audience fit, Recognizably us (score 1-5 each)
For C and L, list every claim, number, offer term and disclosure, and say whether it matches the attached
offer sheet / approved claims (match / mismatch / not in sources).
Be specific and critical. Do not rewrite; list issues in order of severity.
[paste draft]
```

**Before:** "Looks good!" from the same chat that wrote the caption.

**After:** a scored review that flags "40% off everything" as a mismatch with the offer sheet ("up to 40% off selected lines"), a missing #ad, and one banned word, in order of severity. You fix them, then a human approves.

### Build a simple test log

| Date | Asset | Variant | Angle | Result (metric) | Keep/kill |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Feed winning variants back into your example bank. Over time, your templates learn from your audience, not just from you.

### Worked example: a sponsored post review

A US-based fitness creator receives an AI-assisted caption for a protein bar sponsorship:

> "Game-changing protein bar with 20g protein that melts fat while you sleep! Use my code for 50% off"

CLEAR review:

- **Correct:** protein amount confirmed from the pack. "Melts fat while you sleep" is unsupported. Discount is actually 20%. Score 1.
- **Legal:** no sponsorship disclosure; a health claim the brand did not approve; wrong discount. Score 1.
- **Engaging:** decent energy. 3.
- **Audience fit:** OK. 3.
- **Recognisably us:** "game-changing" is on the ban list. 2.

Revised: "#ad I've been keeping these in my gym bag for post-workout snacks: 20g protein and they actually taste like dessert. Code SAM20 gets you 20% off." Plus the platform's paid-partnership label.

### Pitfalls

- Skipping review "just this once" on a busy day.
- Checking only the first draft, not the final revised version.
- Treating AI evaluation as final approval.

lessons.title: Escaping generic AI output: originality techniques
lessons.body:
### The sameness problem

As more people use similar tools with similar prompts, a recognizable "AI voice" has emerged: tidy three-part lists, the same stock openers, predictable metaphors and upbeat conclusions. Audiences scroll past it. Your competitive advantage is whatever the model cannot know: your experiences, customers, opinions and data.

### Tell-tale signs of generic output

- Openers like "In today's fast-paced world" or "Are you ready to take your X to the next level?"
- Over-used words: *elevate, unlock, seamless, game-changer, delve, landscape, journey, empower*.
- Everything in groups of three; every paragraph the same length.
- Vague benefits ("boost your productivity") without a concrete example.
- A neat moral at the end of every post.
- No opinion, no tension, no specifics.

### Seven techniques for original output

**1. Feed it raw material only you have.**
Voice notes, customer DMs (anonymized), sales call quotes, your failures, behind-the-scenes details. "Here is a voice note transcript of me explaining why I quit my job. Turn it into a LinkedIn post. Keep my phrases; don't polish away the rough edges."

**2. Start with your opinion.**
"My contrarian view: most small brands post too often. Write a post defending this view with my reasons: [reasons]."

**3. Demand specifics.**
"Replace every general claim with a specific example, number (from my data only) or story." "Name the exact moment, place or object."

**4. Ban the clichés explicitly.**
Maintain a banned-phrase list in your voice guide and include it in prompts. Ask the model to self-check: "Before finalizing, remove any phrase from the banned list and any sentence that could appear in any brand's post."

**5. Change the form.**
Instead of a standard caption, try a list of mistakes you made, a text-message conversation, a "things I'd tell my younger self" format, or a mini case study with a real (consented) customer.

**6. Use AI for structure, you for the words.**
Ask for an outline, angles or a critique, then write the key lines yourself. Many successful creators use AI mainly for thinking and editing, not final wording.

**7. Edit for rhythm and voice.**
Read it aloud. Vary sentence length. Cut the throat-clearing first sentence. Add the joke only you would make.

### Worked example: from generic to specific

**Generic AI draft (Dubai real estate agent):**
"Looking for your dream home in Dubai? Our expert team is here to guide you through every step of your property journey. Contact us today to unlock the door to your future!"

**Prompt with raw material:**
> Rewrite this using these real details: last month I showed a family 11 villas in Arabian Ranches before they chose the 12th because the kids' bedrooms got morning light. My view: most buyers over-focus on the kitchen and under-focus on commute time at 7:30am. Keep it conversational. Ban: dream, journey, unlock, expert team.

**Result (after light human edit):**
"Last month a family viewed 11 villas with me. They picked number 12, not for the kitchen, but because the kids' rooms got morning sun. Here's what I tell every buyer: drive the school run at 7:30am before you fall in love with a kitchen island. DM me 'COMMUTE' and I'll send you the checklist I use."

(The agent checks that sharing the anecdote does not identify the family.)

### Hands-on: the raw-material rewrite

Collect three pieces of raw material only you have: a voice memo transcript, an anonymized customer message, and a real number from your own data. Then:

```text
Here is a draft post: [paste generic draft].
Rewrite it using ONLY these real details: [voice memo quote], [customer message, anonymized], [real number + source].
Keep my phrases from the voice memo; don't polish away rough edges.
Ban: [your banned list]. No groups of three. No moral at the end.
Before finalizing, remove any sentence that could appear in any other brand's post.
```

**Before:** "In today's fast-paced world, finding the right accountant can be a game-changer for your small business journey."

**After:** "Last April a bakery owner brought me a shoebox of receipts and said, 'I think the tax office hates me.' We sorted it in two afternoons. The shoebox wasn't the problem; not knowing which 11 receipts mattered was. Here's the list." (Every detail is true and used with permission.)

### Use AI for thinking, you for the words

Many strong creators now use assistants mainly to find angles, critique drafts and cut, then write the key lines themselves. Try it for a week: ask for 10 angles and a critique, but write the first and last lines of every post yourself.

### Pitfalls

- **Swapping one cliché for another.** Banning words is not enough; add real specifics.
- **Fake specificity.** Inventing stories or numbers to sound authentic is deception. Use only true details.
- **Losing your voice through over-editing with AI.** Keep some imperfection.
